identification.summary: HiddenArt is the name Enea's AdaptiveMobile Security unit assigned to a mobile-network signalling threat actor (a 'platform') that it believes with a high degree of confidence originates from Russian network sources [S1][S4]. Enea says it sustains a capacity to remotely access the personal devices of targeted individuals worldwide, and periodic reconnaissance was seen in at least 7 target mobile networks [S2]. Enea's presentation describes it as a core-network signalling actor whose main behaviour is location tracking and voice/SMS interception, in bursts with long gaps [S3].
identification.firstObserved: Publicly disclosed February 2022 in the 'Spectrum of Violence' research [S2]. Enea says the 'Hidden' part of the name reflects a feature the platform has used for 5+ years [S2]; the first-detection date is not stated in the sources gathered.
identification.notes: Single-vendor designation (Enea / AdaptiveMobile Security). No MITRE ATT&CK group ID and no Microsoft name were found. Malpedia lists no malware families for it and cites only the 2022 Enea write-up [S4]. A search summary of the Enea blog says the name's 'Art' element refers to the Old Irish word for bear; the blog page could not be opened to confirm [S1].

attribution.sponsor: Enea assesses with a high degree of confidence that HiddenArt originates from Russian network sources [S1]. Enea's sources gathered do not confirm a specific state organization or government control; this is a vendor assessment, not a government attribution.
attribution.confidence: Enea states it believes 'with a high degree of confidence' that the platform originates from Russian network sources [S1][S4]. Enea also notes that the actor's disguise makes attribution much harder [S1].
attribution.basis: Enea correlated signalling data across networks, tracking recurring Global Titles, message sequences and routing paths; individual messages can look like legitimate signalling when seen alone [S1]. The detailed basis for the Russia assessment is not available in the sources I could open [S1].

objectives: Enea describes the activity as location tracking and voice and SMS interception of targeted individuals [S3]. Search summaries of Enea's blog say targets were mainly VIP individuals, many with Russian links [S1]. The actor's ultimate tasking is not stated in the sources gathered.

sectors: Mobile network operators (infrastructure attacked via core signalling) [S2]
Individual subscribers, described by Enea as mainly VIPs [S1]
regions: Global; periodic reconnaissance in at least 7 target mobile networks worldwide [S2]
targeting.notes: Specific operators, countries and victim names are not given in the sources gathered. The AdaptiveMobile white paper frames mobile-network attacks in the context of hybrid warfare [S2].

capabilities.summary: Core-network (SS7) signalling attacks for location tracking and voice/SMS interception, delivered in bursts [S1][S3]. Enea reports the actor tries to make its source SCCP Global Titles as similar as possible to real, non-malicious GTs of legitimate network nodes, which could evade operators with weaker firewalls; the messages appeared to come from GTs linked to a group of African networks [S1]. Enea's presentation also gives a working theory, based on captured traffic, that the actor injects attack requests using spoofed global titles and copies responses to itself [S3]. No malware families are listed [S4].

campaigns.name: Enea/AdaptiveMobile 'Spectrum of Violence' disclosure
campaigns.summary: Enea's AdaptiveMobile Security disclosed HiddenArt, found using its SIGIL signalling intelligence platform, with periodic reconnaissance against at least 7 mobile networks worldwide [S2].

campaigns.name: Enea presentation 'The Hidden Global Battlefield'
campaigns.summary: Presentation hosted by ENISA describes HiddenArt as a core-network signalling actor focused on location tracking and voice/SMS interception, active in bursts. The date comes from the file name only [S3].

diamond.adversary: Unnamed operator of a signalling platform that Enea assesses originates from Russian network sources [S1].
diamond.capability: SS7 location tracking and voice/SMS interception; GT spoofing to resemble legitimate GTs [S1][S3].
diamond.infrastructure: SS7 signalling access appearing from GTs linked to a group of African networks (per Enea blog summary); actual operator access points are not identified [S1].
diamond.victim: Targeted individuals, mainly VIPs per Enea, and at least 7 mobile networks reconnoitred worldwide [S1][S2].
diamond.socioPolitical: Enea places the activity within hybrid-warfare use of mobile networks [S2].
diamond.technology: Legacy SS7 signalling interconnects and operators with weak signalling firewalls [S1].

gaps: Could not open the Enea blog, the Enea press release, the ENISA-hosted slides or the white paper (host unreachable); findings rely on search-result summaries of them. Verify against the primaries before use.
Blog publication date not confirmed; 'Spectrum of Violence' dated February 2022 from the Enea press release listing, and the slide deck date (2022-06) is inferred from its file name [S2][S3].
No government or third-party corroboration of Russian attribution; the basis is a single vendor's assessment [S1].
Victim networks, countries, individual targets and exact first-detection date are not public in the sources gathered.
No malware, tooling or ATT&CK mapping; no overlap analysis with other Russian actors.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Mobile operator core signalling (SS7 interconnect, Global Title translation) is key terrain, and the targets are subscribers' phones reached through it [S1][S2]. STEP 2: The actor operates through the network, not the handset, so device security controls do not see it [S2]. STEP 3: Observed pattern is bursty reconnaissance, then location tracking and voice/SMS interception, using GTs spoofed to resemble legitimate ones [S1][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued covert tracking and interception of VIP individuals across multiple operators. MDCOA is use of the same access to track or intercept deployed personnel or leaders in a crisis or hybrid conflict (the white paper's framing) [S2]. Candidate indicators: recurring GTs and message sequences, location-query bursts on subscribers from unfamiliar GTs, and signalling from GTs resembling legitimate peers [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: personnel and VIP use of commercial mobile networks, especially roaming, is exposed to signalling-layer tracking and interception that the user cannot detect [S1][S2]. (2) Authorities: operator signalling defenses are owned by carriers and regulators, not DoD; DoD action is mostly guidance and coordination [S2]. (3) Mission assurance: avoid reliance on SMS and voice over commercial networks for sensitive coordination and use end-to-end encrypted channels. (4) Coordination: use host-nation and carrier channels and signalling-intelligence sharing for reports of anomalous GTs [S1].

provenance.importedSummary: It was observed that a mobile network threat actor designated as ‘HiddenArt’ actively sustains a capacity to remotely access the personal devices of targeted individuals around the world on an ongoing basis. Since detecting this threat actor, periodic reconnaissance activities were observed in at least 7 target mobile networks around the world and given the wide geographic distribution of these targeted mobile operators, it is probable that the threat actor is active on a global scale.
